title: Premises Access and Audit Authority
summary: This thread tracks the evolution of customs authority to access, inspect, and audit business premises. It transitions from general enforcement powers under the Customs Act to specific, structured audit requirements for Authorized Economic Operators (AEOs) and licensed entities.

evolution.scope: From general search/seizure to specific AEO compliance and security auditing.
evolution.procedure: From ad-hoc inspection to structured system-based audits and physical security checks.

timeline.change: Formalized the requirement for premises ownership or rental documentation as a condition for license application.
Introduced system-based audit requirements for AEOs, including physical inspection of premises.
Expanded audit scope to include on-site physical inspection and coordination with local VAT/Excise offices for warehouse verification.
Added security-focused requirements regarding co-located entities and physical/electronic access control for employees.

Authorized Economic Operator: Audit activities for these entities should focus on system-based audits to ensure regulatory compliance.
When conducting post-clearance audits for these organizations, specific procedures beyond standard practices must be prioritized to verify the accuracy of declarations and internal operations.
H.S. Code: Auditors are required to verify the accuracy of these codes specifically for high-volume and high-value products to prevent misclassification.
Customs Clearance: Physical verification of goods at the premises of the authorized entity should be conducted on a random basis to ensure consistency with declared information.
Customs Computerised Entry Processing Sy: Auditors must inspect the entity's internal databases, computer systems, and software modules, particularly those related to supply chain management, to validate transaction integrity.
Customs Duty: Audit procedures must prioritize verifying the ratio of finished goods produced against total imported inputs to ensure that all relevant duties and taxes have been correctly calculated and paid.

Authorized Economic Operator: A Class-3 recognized institution may request physical examination of their imported or exported goods at the premises of the institution or their warehouse rather than the customs station.

Upon completion of the physical examination by authorized officers, the entity must ensure that the examination report is sent to the relevant customs, excise, and VAT authorities for final processing.
Customs Clearance: The customs clearance process for recognized institutions allows for provisional assessment and release of goods prior to full physical examination.
Final clearance is completed by the customs station only after receiving the examination report from the relevant customs, excise, and VAT division and collecting all applicable duties and taxes.
Customs, Excise and VAT Department: Designated officers from this department are responsible for conducting physical examinations of goods at the recognized institution's premises or warehouse upon request.
This department must submit a formal examination report to the relevant customs station to facilitate the final assessment and clearance of the goods.

Customs Officer: A Customs Officer is authorized to enter premises where customs-related documents are kept to audit and examine records, whether manual or electronic, regarding transaction accuracy and authenticity.

Customs Officers have the right of full and unrestricted access to premises and documents held by licensees, importers, exporters, or other persons to perform their duties or collect duties under the Act.
Customs Officers are empowered to extract or copy any books, documents, or records necessary for the execution of the Act.
Customs Officers are prohibited from entering private residential premises without the consent of the occupant or owner, or without a valid warrant issued under the Act.
Customs Audit: The law establishes a framework for the audit and examination of business records, allowing officials to verify the accuracy and validity of transactions documented in physical or electronic systems.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal mandate for customs authorities to access business premises, audit documentation, and perform inspections to ensure compliance with customs duties and administrative obligations.

Bonded Warehouse Operation: A licensee of a private warehouse is required to allow entry to customs officers and follow their instructions to open the premises for inspection.
Failure to comply with an authorized customs officer's request for entry or refusal to open the warehouse is a punishable offence.
Customs Offence Penalties: A licensee who prevents a customs officer from accessing a private warehouse is liable to a monetary fine.
In addition to a fine, the licensee faces the immediate cancellation of their warehouse license for non-compliance.

Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer is designated as the minimum rank required for authorizing search and seizure operations under this Act.
The officer is also responsible for granting prior authorization for the arrest of individuals suspected of smuggling offences within specific border zones.
Customs Officer: Officers are empowered to conduct searches of premises without a warrant if there is a reasonable belief that relevant goods, documents, or items are concealed there and are at risk of being removed.

In designated border areas, officers are authorized to arrest individuals involved in smuggling, enter premises, seize contraband or relevant evidence, and use necessary force to prevent escape or the removal of illicit goods.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: All search operations conducted under this provision must adhere to the rules and procedures established by this code, subject to necessary modifications.
Government of Bangladesh: The government's written permission is a mandatory requirement before any civil suit, criminal prosecution, or legal action can be initiated against an official for acts performed or intended in the exercise of search and arrest powers.

Customs Offence Penalties: The government may require a person convicted of a customs offence to display a public notice at their place of business detailing the conviction for a minimum period of three months.
Failure to comply with the requirement to display such a notice is deemed a repeat of the original offence for which the person was convicted.
Customs authorities are empowered to enter the premises of a convicted person to affix the required notice if the person refuses or fails to comply with the display mandate.

In cases where a standard notice is deemed insufficient for public awareness, the government may require the convicted person to display a notice in a specific format or font size as prescribed, failure of which also constitutes a repeat offence.

Customs Officer: A Customs Officer is authorized to enter premises where records are kept to audit and examine them in relation to specific transactions or the integrity of the systems used to store them.

A Customs Officer has the power to access lands, buildings, places, books, and documents held by any person to collect duty or perform functions under the Act, including making copies or extracts of such documents.
A Customs Officer is restricted from entering a private dwelling without the consent of the owner or occupier, or unless they have obtained a warrant issued under the Act.
Customs Records Retention: Records that are required to be kept under the Act are subject to audit and examination by an officer of Customs at any time.
Licensee: A licensee must grant the officer of Customs full and free access to their books, records, documents, and premises for the purpose of an audit or examination.
Importer: An importer must provide the officer of Customs with full and free access to their books, records, and documents to facilitate the audit and examination process as required by the Act.
Exporter: An exporter is subject to the authority of a Customs Officer who may examine their records and premises to ensure compliance with duty collection and other legal functions.
Search Warrant: A warrant is required if a Customs Officer intends to enter a private dwelling for the purposes of audit or examination without the consent of the occupant or owner.

Power to search and arrest without warrant.- (1) Whenever any officer or customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] or any other officer 2[* * * *] employed for the prevention of smuggling has reasonable grounds for believing that any goods liable to confiscation or any documents or things which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any proceeding under this Act are concealed or kept in any place and that there is a danger that they may be removed before a search can be effected under section 162, he may, after preparing a statement in writing of the grounds of his belief and of the goods, documents or things for which search is to be made, search or cause of search to be made for such goods, documents or things in that place.
(2) Any officer or person who makes a search or causes a search to be made under sub-section (1) shall leave a signed copy of the aforementioned statement in or about the place searched and shall, at the time the search is made or as soon as is practicable thereafter, deliver furthermore a signed copy of such statement to the occupier of the place at his last known address.
(3) All searches made under this section shall be carried out mutatis mutandis in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898).

Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer is authorized to form beliefs regarding the concealment of goods or documents subject to search and to authorize officers to conduct searches or arrests without a warrant under specified conditions.
Smuggling: The prevention of smuggling is a primary function that empowers customs officers to carry out searches and arrests without a warrant in defined circumstances.
Specific enforcement powers, including the use of force and warrantless entry of premises, are granted to customs officers when dealing with offences related to smuggling.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: All searches conducted under this section must adhere to the procedural requirements established in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Officer of Customs: Officers are empowered to enter and search premises, seize goods suspected of smuggling, and arrest individuals involved in such offences without a warrant under specific conditions.
When necessary to execute duties such as arresting persons or seizing goods, these officers may use force, including lethal force, to prevent escape or the removal of illicit items.
Government: Legal proceedings cannot be instituted against any person acting under the powers granted in this section without the prior written sanction of the Government.
Customs Offence: Special enforcement provisions apply to offences related to smuggling, allowing for warrantless arrests, entry of premises, and the use of force within designated border and coastal zones.
